fetched_contents.text: Biochar production under different pyrolysis temperatures with different types of agricultural wastes Introduction Biochar is a carbon-rich material which is produced by of heating biomass such as wood, manure, or leaves, at temperatures of 400–700 °C in a closed container in which oxygen is absent or depleted1. Biochar is used as an amendment to soil growth media and is produced by the pyrolysis of organic wastes. The pyrolysis process produces biochar and two additional materials—syngas and bio-oil—that have commercial value as energy sources. Recently, biochar has received considerable attention as a soil amendment for increasing agricultural productivity2,3. Alghashm et al4 mentioned that the pyrolysis temperature for preparing biochar ranged from 400 to 900 °C. Jindo et al5 selected some organic wastes (rice husk, rice straw, wood chips of apple tree and oak tree) with different characteristics and were pyrolyzed at different temperatures (400, 500, 600, 700 and 800 °C) in order to optimize the physicochemical properties of biochar as a soil amendment. Scientists and policymakers are beginning to recognize the important role of biochar in the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, production of renewable energy, mitigation of waste, and application as a soil amendment6. Biochar is used in many fields. In agriculture, it is used as an organic fertilizer that degrades over a long time. When added to soil, it positively affects the soil fertility, the total biogenic components, physical and water characteristics, and biological features7,8. The physical characteristics of biochar render it a useful tool for environmental management. The physical properties of biochar can affect soil systems directly and indirectly. Different soils have distinct physical features that are dependent upon the nature and relative quantity of their mineral and organic matter content, as well as the association between the minerals and organic matter9. Biochar added to a soil mixture can significantly contribute to the physical nature of the system by affecting the penetration depth, structure, texture, porosity, and consistency by changing the surface area, particle size distribution, pore size distribution, density, and packing10. The influence of biochar on the physical features of soil can then have a direct impact on plant growth because the penetration depth and availability of air and water in the root zone are largely determined by the physical make-up of the soil horizons. Biochar’s presence in soil directly affect the soil’s response to water, as well as its aggregation, workability during soil preparation, swelling shrinking dynamics, permeability, capacity to retain cations, and response to ambient temperature changes. In addition, many chemical and biological aspects of soil fertility can be indirectly inferred from these physical properties, such as the physical availability of sites for chemical reactions and the provision of protective habitats for soil microbes11,12. Biochar has higher nutrient retention capacity and higher resistance to degradation by microorganisms which are due to chemical and colloidal structure13. Despite of high significant losses of nutrients during pyrolysis, biochar has positive responses on the soil, because it neutralizes the toxins and improves the physical properties of soils such as water retention as well as develop a protection against heavy metal pollution and reduce soil compaction11. Physical and chemical features of biochar vary by the variation of the properties of raw materials used and conditions of pyrolysis14. Soil properties such as physical and biological properties could be improved by using biochar and it is used as preventive against heavy metal stress of soil15,16. Biochar produced from cotton stalk has capacity of holding higher Cadium (Cd) in soil contaminated with Cd. It reduced the biological effect of Cd in soil by changing the morphological structure of Cd17. Several studies have been covered the production of biochar from agriculture wastes which was used to prevent the heavy metals and organic pollutants in soil and water18. Biochar could be used in improving anaerobic digestion as mentioned by Valentin et al19 whose stated that properties such as specific surface area (SSA), cation exchange capacity, presence of functional groups and electrical conductivity were found favorable for increased methane production, reduction of lag phase, and adsorption of inhibitors. The published works on biochar application to soil have predominantly focused on agronomic benefits, while the physical and chemical properties of the produced biochar and their effects on soil structure and texture have received little attention. How temperature changes the chemical composition of biochar

The evidence points to a clear temperature-dependent evolution of biochar chemistry, with functional groups, oxygen content, aromaticity, and pyrolysis-stage decomposition all changing as temperature increases. Across the search results, biochar produced at higher pyrolysis temperatures is associated with lower concentrations of hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and labile organic carbon, while more resistant carbon structures dominate [N1-R2]. A separate search result similarly states that as pyrolysis temperature increases, weaker-bonded groups are progressively released, forming larger polyaromatic structures with lower hydrogen and oxygen [N1-R5]. This is consistent with the idea that higher temperature favors the condensation and aromatization of carbon, reducing the proportion of oxygen-containing functional groups and labile organics [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Functional groups are a central part of this compositional shift. The characterization literature notes that SEM, TEM, FTIR, BET surface area, and pore volume are commonly used to examine biochar structure, and FTIR spectra in one study revealed surface groups such as hydroxyls at ~3328 cm⁻¹, carboxyls at ~1703 cm⁻¹, and C=O or C=C contributions at ~1532 cm⁻¹ [N3-F3]. In the same context, the presence of hydroxyl, carboxyl, and other surface groups is tied to adsorption capacity because these groups interact with metals via hydrogen bonding and complexation [N3-F3]. The DFT-based review further emphasizes that functional groups such as hydroxyl (−OH), amino (−NH2), and carboxyl (−COOH) strongly influence biochar physicochemical properties and its interactions with soil substances [N5-F2]. This suggests that as temperature changes, these functional groups either persist, diminish, or restructure depending on the pyrolysis stage.

Aromaticity and oxygen content evolve in a predictable way across temperature ranges. Lower temperatures are associated with greater oxygen content, more functional groups, and higher hydrogen and oxygen concentrations, while higher temperatures are linked to lower oxygen content, greater aromatic carbon, and more recalcitrant structures [N1-R2][N1-R5]. The review explicitly states that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, whereas higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and a higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. This supports the conclusion that aromaticity tends to increase with temperature, while oxygen content decreases [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Evidence for pyrolysis-stage effects on chemical composition comes from multiple sources. One study notes that primary decomposition occurs in the temperature range of 200–350°C, while secondary degradation starts above 400°C [N1-R4]. Another study reports that increasing pyrolysis temperature progressively degrades organic matter and removes pore material, which is directly relevant to chemical composition changes [N2-R3]. The DFT review also frames pyrolysis temperature as the most significant manufacturing condition affecting biochar properties, with lower temperatures preserving functional groups and higher temperatures promoting recalcitrant carbon [N5-F2]. Together, these sources support a staged model of biochar formation: early-stage decomposition at lower temperatures releases labile organics and functional groups, while higher temperatures drive further aromatization and stabilization of carbon [N1-R4][N2-R3][N5-F2].

Temperature-dependent decomposition phases affect composition by altering the pathways through which biomass is converted. The evidence suggests that at lower temperatures, more volatile and labile components are retained, whereas at higher temperatures, volatiles are removed and carbonization proceeds, favoring aromatic and graphitic structures [N1-R4][N1-R5]. The comparison study also states that higher pyrolysis temperature produced products with higher organic carbon and a more developed structure, while lower temperature had lower yield and different properties [N4-R4]. This implies that decomposition phases are not simply thermal degradation but are also shaped by whether the system is in the primary or secondary pyrolysis regime [N1-R4][N4-R4].

Overall, the chemical composition of biochar changes systematically with pyrolysis temperature: lower temperatures preserve more oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and labile organics and retain functional groups; higher temperatures reduce these elements and increase aromaticity, recalcitrant carbon, and surface stability [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-F2]. The evidence supports a clear pyrolysis-stage effect, with composition depending on whether the temperature is in the primary decomposition range, secondary degradation range, or carbonization range [N1-R4][N2-R3][N5-F2].
node_outputs.N8:
How temperature changes the pore structure and porosity of biochar

The evidence indicates that pyrolysis temperature has a strong influence on pore size distribution and porosity, with distinct pore types dominating at low, medium, and high temperatures. Across the search results, temperature is linked to changes in porosity and pore size distribution, and one study notes that biochar yield decreases with increasing pyrolysis temperature, with analyzed properties varying accordingly [N4-R1]. Another study reports that higher pyrolysis temperature resulted in lower yields but higher organic carbon content and a more developed structure [N4-R4], while a related search result says that higher pyrolysis temperatures generally enhance biochar porosity by removing volatiles and promoting the condensation of amorphous C into crystalline forms [N2-R4]. The 4D structural changes study further states that pyrolysis temperature played a role in creating variations in pore size distribution of biochar, generally at temperatures below 550°C [N2-R1]. Taken together, these sources support a consistent pattern: temperature controls both the magnitude and distribution of porosity.

Pore size distribution varies with temperature. The evidence does not provide a single temperature-coded pore-type hierarchy across all studies, but it does support a general progression. At lower temperatures, the structure may retain more volatiles and weaker bonds, which can contribute to the formation of meso- and macropores, while higher temperatures drive the removal of volatiles and the condensation of carbon, favoring mesopore development and potentially increasing surface area [N2-R4][N2-R1]. The comparison study on agricultural waste biochar specifically mentions that physical properties such as porosity were analyzed across pyrolysis temperatures, which directly supports the relevance of temperature to pore structure [N4-F1]. The characterization literature also notes that SEM, TEM, FTIR, BET surface area, and pore volume are used to examine biochar structure, showing that porosity is a measurable and routinely studied parameter [N3-F3].

The dominant pore types appear to shift with temperature. The evidence does not identify a single universal pore-type hierarchy across all studies, but it does indicate that mesopores are especially responsive to pyrolysis conditions. One study says that higher pyrolysis temperatures generally enhance porosity by removing volatiles and promoting the condensation of amorphous C into crystalline forms [N2-R4]. Another study says that at temperatures below 550°C, pore size distribution varies with pyrolysis temperature [N2-R1]. A separate source states that increasing pyrolysis temperature progressively degrades organic matter and removes pore material, which is relevant to the relationship between temperature and pore structure [N2-R3]. These findings suggest that mesopores may dominate in the intermediate temperature range, while lower temperatures may preserve more open structures and higher temperatures may condense the structure into denser, more crystalline forms [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

Thermal degradation and carbonization influence structure by altering the balance between volatiles, carbon, and pore geometry. The evidence shows that as temperature increases, volatiles are removed and amorphous carbon condenses, which can increase porosity and refine pore size distribution [N2-R4]. The same source also links increasing pyrolysis temperature to progressively degrading organic matter and removing pore material [N2-R3]. This indicates that thermal degradation reduces the amount of pore-forming material, while carbonization can either refine or condense pore structures depending on the temperature stage [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The comparison study also states that higher pyrolysis temperature produced products with higher organic carbon and a more developed structure, which is consistent with a carbonization-driven shift in structure [N4-R4].

Yield and volatiles affect observed porosity because lower yield is associated with higher temperature, and higher temperature is associated with greater volatile removal and more carbonization [N4-R1][N2-R4]. The evidence on agricultural waste biochar explicitly analyzes physical properties such as porosity across pyrolysis temperatures, reinforcing that temperature is a key driver of porosity changes [N4-F1]. In addition, the characterization literature notes that SEM, TEM, FTIR, BET surface area, and pore volume are used to examine biochar structure, which means that porosity is often measured as a composite of surface area, pore volume, and pore size distribution [N3-F3]. This makes yield and volatiles confounding variables in porosity interpretation: higher temperature lowers yield, removes volatiles, and may increase or refine porosity depending on the stage of carbonization [N4-R1][N2-R4].

In summary, pyrolysis temperature changes the pore structure and porosity of biochar by altering pore size distribution, with mesopores often showing the strongest temperature sensitivity. Lower temperatures may preserve more open structures and functional groups, while higher temperatures drive volatile removal, carbonization, and the formation of denser or more refined pores [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The evidence supports a staged interpretation: temperature controls whether the material is in a volatile-rich, early-decomposition regime or a carbonization-dominated regime, with yield and volatiles acting as secondary variables that affect the observed porosity [N4-R1][N2-R4].
node_outputs.N9:
How experimental conditions and feedstock affect observed temperature effects

Feedstock type moderates pyrolysis temperature effects in several ways. The evidence shows that different feedstocks can produce biochars with very different chemical and structural responses to temperature. The DFT-based review explicitly states that biochar derived from wood-based feedstock exhibits superior physical characteristics such as increased porosity and specific surface area, whereas biochar derived from straw-based feedstock contains excellent element content such as O, N, and H [N5-F2]. It also says that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, while higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and a higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. This indicates that feedstock composition and type strongly influence which temperature range produces the most desirable properties, such as high porosity, high surface area, or high oxygen content [N5-F2].

Operational differences between studies make comparisons valid only when temperature ranges, feedstocks, and characterization methods are comparable. The comparison study on agricultural waste biochar explicitly analyzes physical and chemical properties across pyrolysis temperatures and uses the same four materials (straw rice, sawdust, sugar cane plant residues, and tree leaves) under controlled conditions [N4-F1]. The review on feedstock and pyrolysis conditions also emphasizes that biochar yield is significantly influenced by operating temperature around 500°C, which corresponds to lignin decomposition or elimination of volatile matter [N5-R3]. This suggests that valid comparisons require attention to temperature windows, feedstock identity, and process conditions, because otherwise differences in yield, functional groups, and porosity can be misattributed to temperature alone [N4-F1][N5-R3].

Temperature ranges are typically defined in biochar literature as broad, overlapping intervals rather than exact thresholds. The evidence shows that pyrolysis temperature is often reported in ranges such as 200–350°C, 300–350°C, 400–500°C, 450–750°C, and 300–900°C, with some sources specifying subranges for primary and secondary decomposition [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The review on recent advancements also states that fast pyrolysis is carried out at 450 to 600°C with a relatively higher heating rate, while slower processes may fall outside this range [N6-R4]. This indicates that temperature ranges are commonly used as approximate operational windows, not fixed cutoffs, and that studies often define them based on feedstock behavior, process design, or the point at which decomposition or carbonization becomes dominant [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4].

Yield and other process variables interact with temperature effects in several ways. First, yield is inversely related to temperature in the evidence: higher pyrolysis temperature results in lower yield, while lower temperature can preserve more volatiles and functional groups [N4-R1][N4-R4]. Second, volatile removal is a key factor in porosity and structure, because removing volatiles can increase porosity but also reduce the amount of material available for carbonization [N2-R4]. Third, heating rate and retention time are mentioned as important process variables that interact with temperature. One study notes that the objective was to determine interrelationships among temperature, material grain size, heating rate, and retention time [N2-R2], while another states that pyrolysis temperature and pyrolytic atmosphere have substantial influence on biochar yield and surface functional groups [N5-F2]. This means that temperature effects cannot be interpreted in isolation; they must be considered alongside yield, volatiles, heating rate, and retention time [N2-R2][N4-R1][N5-F2].

The evidence also shows that feedstock and pyrolysis conditions are the primary factors determining biochar stability and properties. The review states that biochar stability is likely related primarily to feedstock type and pyrolysis conditions, followed by secondary environmental factors [N5-R2]. It also states that biochar properties are mainly determined by feedstock physicochemical properties and pyrolytic temperature [N5-F2]. This implies that feedstock and process conditions are not just background variables; they are central to explaining why temperature effects differ between studies. For example, wood-based feedstock may respond to higher temperature with greater recalcitrant carbon and porosity, while straw-based feedstock may preserve more oxygen and functional groups at lower temperatures [N5-F2].

In short, feedstock type moderates temperature effects by altering the baseline chemistry, porosity, and functional groups available for pyrolysis [N5-F2]. Operational differences, including temperature range definitions, heating rate, retention time, and yield, make comparisons valid only when these variables are comparable across studies [N2-R2][N4-F1][N5-R3]. Temperature ranges are usually defined broadly as decomposition or carbonization windows rather than exact thresholds [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R5]. Yield and other process variables interact with temperature by affecting porosity, volatiles, and surface functional groups, meaning that temperature effects must be interpreted in the context of the entire pyrolysis system [N4-R1][N2-R4][N5-F2].
node_outputs.N10:
A concise summary of temperature-dependent biochar properties across studies

Consensus findings across multiple studies show that higher pyrolysis temperature generally reduces yield and increases organic carbon, porosity, and recalcitrant carbon, while lower temperature tends to preserve more oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and labile organics and retain more functional groups [N4-R1][N4-R4][N5-F2]. The evidence also consistently associates higher temperature with lower hydrogen and oxygen content, more aromaticity, and greater specific surface area or porosity [N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-R4][N5-F2]. A common theme is that temperature determines whether the material is in an early-decomposition regime or a carbonization-dominated regime, with the primary decomposition range often around 200–350°C and secondary degradation above 400°C [N1-R4].

Where studies disagree or show mixed results, the evidence suggests differences in feedstock and process conditions rather than fundamental inconsistency. For example, the comparison study on agricultural waste biochar explicitly analyzes physical and chemical properties across pyrolysis temperatures but does not report conflicting conclusions on temperature trends; instead, it emphasizes that physical and chemical properties vary with temperature and that feedstock choice affects the resulting properties [N4-F1]. The DFT-based review also notes that while qualitative correlations between pyrolysis temperature, feedstock properties, and biochar characteristics are established, there is still uncertainty regarding adjustment of production conditions and the exact relationships [N5-F2]. This implies that some studies may differ because they use different feedstocks, temperature windows, or pyrolysis atmospheres, rather than because temperature effects themselves are inconsistent [N5-F2].

The properties most consistently affected by temperature are yield, oxygen content, aromaticity, porosity, surface area, and functional-group density. The evidence repeatedly shows that higher temperature lowers yield and reduces hydrogen and oxygen, while increasing organic carbon, porosity, and recalcitrant carbon [N4-R1][N4-R4][N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-R4]. It also consistently links temperature to changes in surface groups and adsorption sites, indicating that functional-group density is another consistent variable [N3-F3][N5-F2]. The literature also consistently points to porosity and pore size distribution as temperature-sensitive properties [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Limitations and confounders remain in the literature. First, feedstock type strongly moderates temperature effects, so comparisons across studies may be invalid if feedstock differences are not controlled [N5-F2][N5-R2]. Second, temperature ranges are often defined broadly or operationally rather than as exact thresholds, which makes it difficult to compare results across studies [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R5]. Third, yield and volatiles interact with temperature effects, so lower yield at higher temperature can obscure whether the observed properties are due to temperature alone or to the loss of volatiles and functional groups [N4-R1][N2-R4]. Fourth, the evidence indicates that pyrolysis conditions such as heating rate, retention time, and pyrolytic atmosphere also influence biochar yield and surface functional groups, so temperature effects cannot be isolated from these variables [N2-R2][N5-F2]. Finally, the literature itself acknowledges uncertainty about the exact adjustment of production conditions and the precise relationship between temperature and biochar properties [N5-F2].

Overall, the consensus is that temperature has a clear directionality: higher temperature generally increases recalcitrant carbon, porosity, and surface area while decreasing yield, hydrogen, oxygen, and labile organics. However, the exact temperature effects depend heavily on feedstock, temperature range, and other process variables, which means that the literature remains somewhat mixed in comparison studies and that temperature should be interpreted alongside these confounders [N4-F1][N5-F2][N5-R2].

Integrated explanation of how varying pyrolysis temperature affects chemical composition and pore structure of biochar

## 1) Core temperature-dependent trend: higher temperature usually increases recalcitrant carbon, porosity, and surface area while decreasing yield, hydrogen, oxygen, and labile organics

The branch reports converge on a clear directionality: as pyrolysis temperature increases, biochar becomes more carbon-rich, more porous, and more aromatic, while its yield, hydrogen content, oxygen content, nitrogen content, and labile organic carbon content generally decrease [N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-R1][N4-R4]. This is not a simple linear effect, but a staged transformation in which the material moves from preserving volatile and labile components at lower temperatures to forming more stable, aromatic carbon structures at higher temperatures [N1-R4][N1-R5][N2-R3].

The chemical composition report emphasizes that higher pyrolysis temperature reduces concentrations of hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and labile organic carbon while increasing resistant carbon [N1-R2]. It also says that weaker-bonded groups are progressively released at higher temperatures, forming larger polyaromatic structures with lower hydrogen and oxygen [N1-R5]. The DFT-based review reinforces this by stating that wood-based feedstock tends to yield biochar with more recalcitrant carbon and higher specific surface area, while straw-based feedstock preserves more oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen at lower temperatures [N5-F2]. Taken together, these sources support a consistent picture: higher temperature favors carbonization and aromatization, whereas lower temperature favors retention of labile organics and oxygen-rich functional groups [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-F2].

## 2) Functional groups and surface chemistry change with temperature

The evidence shows that pyrolysis temperature alters the functional groups and surface groups present on biochar. The characterization literature notes that FTIR spectra reveal surface groups such as hydroxyls at ~3328 cm⁻¹, carboxyls at ~1703 cm⁻¹, and C=O or C=C contributions at ~1532 cm⁻¹ [N3-F3]. It also notes that surface hydroxyl, carboxyl, and other groups increase adsorption capacity by enabling hydrogen bonding and complexation with metals [N3-F3]. The chemical composition report adds that higher temperature reduces labile organics and weaker-bonded groups, which is consistent with the idea that higher temperature progressively removes or restructures surface functional groups [N1-R2][N1-R5].

The DFT-based review explicitly identifies hydroxyl (−OH), amino (−NH2), and carboxyl (−COOH) as the main surface groups that influence biochar physicochemical properties and interactions with soil substances [N5-F2]. It also notes that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, while higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and a higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. This means that temperature does not only change the amount of oxygen-containing groups; it also changes which groups remain and how they are spatially organized on the surface [N3-F3][N5-F2].

## 3) Aromaticity and oxygen content evolve in a predictable way across temperature ranges

The branch reports show that aromaticity increases and oxygen content decreases as pyrolysis temperature rises. The chemical composition report says that increasing temperature progressively degrades organic matter and removes pore material, which is directly relevant to the formation of more aromatic, less oxygenated structures [N2-R3]. It also states that primary decomposition occurs in the temperature range of 200–350°C, while secondary degradation starts above 400°C [N1-R4].

The DFT-based review adds that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups and charge-transfer potential, whereas higher temperatures promote recalcitrant carbon and higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. This supports the idea that oxygen content and aromaticity follow a temperature-dependent trajectory: lower temperature preserves more oxygen and labile organics; higher temperature reduces oxygen and increases aromatic carbon [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-F2].

## 4) Pore structure and porosity change with temperature

The pore structure report shows that pyrolysis temperature strongly influences pore size distribution and porosity. The evidence indicates that temperature plays a role in creating variations in the pore size distribution of biochar, especially at temperatures below 550°C [N2-R1]. It also says that higher pyrolysis temperatures generally enhance porosity by removing volatiles and promoting the condensation of amorphous carbon into crystalline forms [N2-R4]. Another source says that increasing pyrolysis temperature progressively degrades organic matter and removes pore material [N2-R3].

Taken together, these findings suggest a general progression: lower temperatures may preserve more open structures and weaker bonds that contribute to porosity, while higher temperatures drive volatile removal and carbonization, which can either refine or condense the pore structure [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The comparison study on agricultural waste biochar explicitly analyzes porosity across pyrolysis temperatures, reinforcing that porosity is a temperature-sensitive property [N4-F1].

## 5) Which pore types dominate at low, medium, and high temperatures?

While the evidence does not provide a single universal hierarchy, it does support a staged interpretation. At lower temperatures, the structure may retain more volatiles and weaker bonds, which can contribute to the formation of meso- and macropores [N2-R1]. At intermediate temperatures, the pore size distribution is strongly affected by pyrolysis temperature, and higher temperatures tend to increase porosity by removing volatiles and condensing amorphous carbon [N2-R1][N2-R4]. At higher temperatures, carbonization becomes dominant, and pore material is progressively degraded, which can reduce pore volume while refining pore size or promoting denser carbon structures [N2-R3][N2-R4].

The evidence also suggests that mesopores are especially sensitive to temperature changes. One source explicitly says that higher pyrolysis temperatures generally enhance porosity by removing volatiles and promoting the condensation of amorphous C into crystalline forms, which is consistent with mesopore development [N2-R4]. Another source says that increasing pyrolysis temperature progressively degrades organic matter and removes pore material, implying that pore structure becomes increasingly defined as temperature rises [N2-R3]. This means that mesopores may dominate in the intermediate temperature range, while lower temperatures may preserve more open structures and higher temperatures may condense the structure into denser or more crystalline forms [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

## 6) Thermal degradation and carbonization influence structure

Thermal degradation and carbonization are the main mechanisms through which pyrolysis temperature affects pore structure. The evidence shows that as temperature increases, volatiles are removed and amorphous carbon condenses into more crystalline forms, which can increase porosity and refine pore size distribution [N2-R4]. It also says that increasing pyrolysis temperature progressively degrades organic matter and removes pore material [N2-R3]. This means that thermal degradation reduces the amount of pore-forming material, while carbonization can either refine or condense pore structures depending on the temperature stage [N2-R3][N2-R4].

The comparison study further states that higher pyrolysis temperature produced products with higher organic carbon and a more developed structure, which is consistent with a carbonization-driven shift in structure [N4-R4]. In other words, higher temperature is associated with more carbonized, more developed structures rather than more volatile-rich structures [N4-R4].

## 7) Yield and volatiles affect observed porosity

Yield and volatiles are important confounding variables in interpreting porosity changes. The evidence shows that higher pyrolysis temperature generally lowers yield [N4-R1][N4-R4]. It also says that higher temperature removes volatiles and promotes the condensation of amorphous carbon into crystalline forms, which can increase porosity [N2-R4]. The comparison study explicitly analyzes porosity across pyrolysis temperatures, showing that porosity is a measurable and temperature-sensitive property [N4-F1].

The practical implication is that observed porosity may be influenced not only by temperature but also by how much material is retained. Lower yield at higher temperature can obscure whether the observed porosity is due to temperature alone or to the loss of volatiles and functional groups [N4-R1][N2-R4]. Similarly, volatile removal can increase porosity, but it may also reduce the amount of carbon available for dense or crystalline structures [N2-R4].

## 8) Feedstock type moderates temperature effects

Feedstock type is a major moderator of how pyrolysis temperature affects biochar. The DFT-based review states that wood-based feedstock tends to yield biochar with higher porosity and specific surface area, while straw-based feedstock contains excellent element content such as O, N, and H [N5-F2]. It also says that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, whereas higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. This means that the same temperature range can produce very different biochars depending on the feedstock.

The comparison study on agricultural waste biochar reinforces this by analyzing physical and chemical properties across pyrolysis temperatures using the same four materials under controlled conditions [N4-F1]. The review on feedstock and pyrolysis conditions also emphasizes that biochar yield is significantly influenced by operating temperature around 500°C, which corresponds to lignin decomposition or elimination of volatile matter [N5-R3]. This shows that feedstock and process conditions are not just background variables; they are central to explaining why temperature effects differ between studies [N4-F1][N5-R3].

## 9) Operational differences and temperature-range definitions make comparisons valid

The evidence indicates that operational differences must be controlled for when comparing biochar properties across temperature studies. The comparison study explicitly uses a controlled set of materials and analyzes properties across pyrolysis temperatures [N4-F1]. The feedstock and pyrolysis conditions review also emphasizes that biochar yield is significantly influenced by operating temperature around 500°C [N5-R3]. This suggests that valid comparisons require attention to temperature windows, feedstock identity, and process conditions, because otherwise differences in yield, functional groups, and porosity can be misattributed to temperature alone [N4-F1][N5-R3].

Temperature ranges in the literature are often defined broadly rather than as exact thresholds. The evidence shows that pyrolysis temperature is reported in ranges such as 200–350°C, 300–350°C, 400–500°C, 450–750°C, and 300–900°C, with some sources specifying subranges for primary decomposition and secondary degradation [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The review on recent advancements states that fast pyrolysis is carried out at 450 to 600°C with a relatively higher heating rate, while slower processes may fall outside this range [N6-R4]. This means that temperature ranges are typically used as approximate operational windows, not fixed cutoffs [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R5].

## 10) Consensus, disagreement, and limitations in the literature

The literature consensus is clear: higher pyrolysis temperature generally reduces yield, lowers hydrogen and oxygen content, increases organic carbon, porosity, and recalcitrant carbon, and increases aromaticity and surface area [N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-R1][N4-R4][N2-R4][N5-F2]. The pore structure report also shows that pore size distribution and porosity vary systematically with temperature [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Where studies disagree or show mixed results, the evidence suggests that the differences are usually due to feedstock, process conditions, temperature window, or pyrolysis atmosphere rather than fundamental inconsistency in the temperature trend [N5-F2][N4-F1]. The DFT-based review explicitly notes that while qualitative correlations between pyrolysis temperature, feedstock properties, and biochar characteristics are established, there is still uncertainty about the exact adjustment of production conditions and the precise relationships [N5-F2].

The most consistently affected properties across studies are yield, oxygen content, aromaticity, porosity, surface area, and functional-group density [N4-R1][N4-R4][N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-R4]. The literature also consistently points to porosity and pore size distribution as temperature-sensitive properties [N2-R1][N2-R4].

## 11) Limitations and confounders remain

Several limitations remain in the literature. First, feedstock type strongly moderates temperature effects, so comparisons across studies may be invalid if feedstock differences are not controlled [N5-F2][N5-R2]. Second, temperature ranges are often defined broadly or operationally rather than as exact thresholds, which makes it difficult to compare results across studies [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R5]. Third, yield and volatiles interact with temperature effects, so lower yield at higher temperature can obscure whether the observed properties are due to temperature alone or to the loss of volatiles and functional groups [N4-R1][N2-R4]. Fourth, the evidence indicates that heating rate, retention time, and pyrolytic atmosphere also influence biochar yield and surface functional groups, so temperature effects cannot be isolated from these variables [N2-R2][N5-F2]. Finally, the literature itself acknowledges uncertainty about the exact adjustment of production conditions and the precise relationship between temperature and biochar properties [N5-F2].

## 12) Bottom line

Overall, varying pyrolysis temperature has a systematic effect on biochar: lower temperature preserves more oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and labile organics, while higher temperature favors recalcitrant carbon, aromaticity, and more developed porosity [N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-R1][N4-R4]. The same temperature change also alters pore structure, with mesopores and porosity often increasing at higher temperatures and pore material progressively being degraded as carbonization proceeds [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. However, feedstock type, temperature range definitions, yield, volatiles, heating rate, and retention time all interact with temperature effects, so the exact outcome depends on the entire pyrolysis system [N5-F2][N5-R3][N6-R1][N6-R5]. The literature therefore supports a staged interpretation of biochar formation, rather than a single universal temperature-response curve [N1-R4][N2-R3][N5-F2].

How temperature changes the chemical composition of biochar

The evidence points to a clear temperature-dependent evolution of biochar chemistry, with functional groups, oxygen content, aromaticity, and pyrolysis-stage decomposition all changing as temperature increases. Across the search results, biochar produced at higher pyrolysis temperatures is associated with lower concentrations of hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and labile organic carbon, while more resistant carbon structures dominate [N1-R2]. A separate search result similarly states that as pyrolysis temperature increases, weaker-bonded groups are progressively released, forming larger polyaromatic structures with lower hydrogen and oxygen [N1-R5]. This is consistent with the idea that higher temperature favors the condensation and aromatization of carbon, reducing the proportion of oxygen-containing functional groups and labile organics [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Functional groups are a central part of this compositional shift. The characterization literature notes that SEM, TEM, FTIR, BET surface area, and pore volume are commonly used to examine biochar structure, and FTIR spectra in one study revealed surface groups such as hydroxyls at ~3328 cm⁻¹, carboxyls at ~1703 cm⁻¹, and C=O or C=C contributions at ~1532 cm⁻¹ [N3-F3]. In the same context, the presence of hydroxyl, carboxyl, and other surface groups is tied to adsorption capacity because these groups interact with metals via hydrogen bonding and complexation [N3-F3]. The DFT-based review further emphasizes that functional groups such as hydroxyl (−OH), amino (−NH2), and carboxyl (−COOH) strongly influence biochar physicochemical properties and its interactions with soil substances [N5-F2]. This suggests that as temperature changes, these functional groups either persist, diminish, or restructure depending on the pyrolysis stage.

Aromaticity and oxygen content evolve in a predictable way across temperature ranges. Lower temperatures are associated with greater oxygen content, more functional groups, and higher hydrogen and oxygen concentrations, while higher temperatures are linked to lower oxygen content, greater aromatic carbon, and more recalcitrant structures [N1-R2][N1-R5]. The review explicitly states that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, whereas higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and a higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. This supports the conclusion that aromaticity tends to increase with temperature, while oxygen content decreases [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Evidence for pyrolysis-stage effects on chemical composition comes from multiple sources. One study notes that primary decomposition occurs in the temperature range of 200–350°C, while secondary degradation starts above 400°C [N1-R4]. Another study reports that increasing pyrolysis temperature progressively degrades organic matter and removes pore material, which is directly relevant to chemical composition changes [N2-R3]. The DFT review also frames pyrolysis temperature as the most significant manufacturing condition affecting biochar properties, with lower temperatures preserving functional groups and higher temperatures promoting recalcitrant carbon [N5-F2]. Together, these sources support a staged model of biochar formation: early-stage decomposition at lower temperatures releases labile organics and functional groups, while higher temperatures drive further aromatization and stabilization of carbon [N1-R4][N2-R3][N5-F2].

Temperature-dependent decomposition phases affect composition by altering the pathways through which biomass is converted. The evidence suggests that at lower temperatures, more volatile and labile components are retained, whereas at higher temperatures, volatiles are removed and carbonization proceeds, favoring aromatic and graphitic structures [N1-R4][N1-R5]. The comparison study also states that higher pyrolysis temperature produced products with higher organic carbon and a more developed structure, while lower temperature had lower yield and different properties [N4-R4]. This implies that decomposition phases are not simply thermal degradation but are also shaped by whether the system is in the primary or secondary pyrolysis regime [N1-R4][N4-R4].

Overall, the chemical composition of biochar changes systematically with pyrolysis temperature: lower temperatures preserve more oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and labile organics and retain functional groups; higher temperatures reduce these elements and increase aromaticity, recalcitrant carbon, and surface stability [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-F2]. The evidence supports a clear pyrolysis-stage effect, with composition depending on whether the temperature is in the primary decomposition range, secondary degradation range, or carbonization range [N1-R4][N2-R3][N5-F2].

How experimental conditions and feedstock affect observed temperature effects

Feedstock type moderates pyrolysis temperature effects in several ways. The evidence shows that different feedstocks can produce biochars with very different chemical and structural responses to temperature. The DFT-based review explicitly states that biochar derived from wood-based feedstock exhibits superior physical characteristics such as increased porosity and specific surface area, whereas biochar derived from straw-based feedstock contains excellent element content such as O, N, and H [N5-F2]. It also says that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, while higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and a higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. This indicates that feedstock composition and type strongly influence which temperature range produces the most desirable properties, such as high porosity, high surface area, or high oxygen content [N5-F2].

Operational differences between studies make comparisons valid only when temperature ranges, feedstocks, and characterization methods are comparable. The comparison study on agricultural waste biochar explicitly analyzes physical and chemical properties across pyrolysis temperatures and uses the same four materials (straw rice, sawdust, sugar cane plant residues, and tree leaves) under controlled conditions [N4-F1]. The review on feedstock and pyrolysis conditions also emphasizes that biochar yield is significantly influenced by operating temperature around 500°C, which corresponds to lignin decomposition or elimination of volatile matter [N5-R3]. This suggests that valid comparisons require attention to temperature windows, feedstock identity, and process conditions, because otherwise differences in yield, functional groups, and porosity can be misattributed to temperature alone [N4-F1][N5-R3].

Temperature ranges are typically defined in biochar literature as broad, overlapping intervals rather than exact thresholds. The evidence shows that pyrolysis temperature is often reported in ranges such as 200–350°C, 300–350°C, 400–500°C, 450–750°C, and 300–900°C, with some sources specifying subranges for primary and secondary decomposition [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The review on recent advancements also states that fast pyrolysis is carried out at 450 to 600°C with a relatively higher heating rate, while slower processes may fall outside this range [N6-R4]. This indicates that temperature ranges are commonly used as approximate operational windows, not fixed cutoffs, and that studies often define them based on feedstock behavior, process design, or the point at which decomposition or carbonization becomes dominant [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4].

Yield and other process variables interact with temperature effects in several ways. First, yield is inversely related to temperature in the evidence: higher pyrolysis temperature results in lower yield, while lower temperature can preserve more volatiles and functional groups [N4-R1][N4-R4]. Second, volatile removal is a key factor in porosity and structure, because removing volatiles can increase porosity but also reduce the amount of material available for carbonization [N2-R4]. Third, heating rate and retention time are mentioned as important process variables that interact with temperature. One study notes that the objective was to determine interrelationships among temperature, material grain size, heating rate, and retention time [N2-R2], while another states that pyrolysis temperature and pyrolytic atmosphere have substantial influence on biochar yield and surface functional groups [N5-F2]. This means that temperature effects cannot be interpreted in isolation; they must be considered alongside yield, volatiles, heating rate, and retention time [N2-R2][N4-R1][N5-F2].

The evidence also shows that feedstock and pyrolysis conditions are the primary factors determining biochar stability and properties. The review states that biochar stability is likely related primarily to feedstock type and pyrolysis conditions, followed by secondary environmental factors [N5-R2]. It also states that biochar properties are mainly determined by feedstock physicochemical properties and pyrolytic temperature [N5-F2]. This implies that feedstock and process conditions are not just background variables; they are central to explaining why temperature effects differ between studies. For example, wood-based feedstock may respond to higher temperature with greater recalcitrant carbon and porosity, while straw-based feedstock may preserve more oxygen and functional groups at lower temperatures [N5-F2].

In short, feedstock type moderates temperature effects by altering the baseline chemistry, porosity, and functional groups available for pyrolysis [N5-F2]. Operational differences, including temperature range definitions, heating rate, retention time, and yield, make comparisons valid only when these variables are comparable across studies [N2-R2][N4-F1][N5-R3]. Temperature ranges are usually defined broadly as decomposition or carbonization windows rather than exact thresholds [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R5]. Yield and other process variables interact with temperature by affecting porosity, volatiles, and surface functional groups, meaning that temperature effects must be interpreted in the context of the entire pyrolysis system [N4-R1][N2-R4][N5-F2].

A concise summary of temperature-dependent biochar properties across studies

Consensus findings across multiple studies show that higher pyrolysis temperature generally reduces yield and increases organic carbon, porosity, and recalcitrant carbon, while lower temperature tends to preserve more oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and labile organics and retain more functional groups [N4-R1][N4-R4][N5-F2]. The evidence also consistently associates higher temperature with lower hydrogen and oxygen content, more aromaticity, and greater specific surface area or porosity [N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-R4][N5-F2]. A common theme is that temperature determines whether the material is in an early-decomposition regime or a carbonization-dominated regime, with the primary decomposition range often around 200–350°C and secondary degradation above 400°C [N1-R4].

Where studies disagree or show mixed results, the evidence suggests differences in feedstock and process conditions rather than fundamental inconsistency. For example, the comparison study on agricultural waste biochar explicitly analyzes physical and chemical properties across pyrolysis temperatures but does not report conflicting conclusions on temperature trends; instead, it emphasizes that physical and chemical properties vary with temperature and that feedstock choice affects the resulting properties [N4-F1]. The DFT-based review also notes that while qualitative correlations between pyrolysis temperature, feedstock properties, and biochar characteristics are established, there is still uncertainty regarding adjustment of production conditions and the exact relationships [N5-F2]. This implies that some studies may differ because they use different feedstocks, temperature windows, or pyrolysis atmospheres, rather than because temperature effects themselves are inconsistent [N5-F2].

The properties most consistently affected by temperature are yield, oxygen content, aromaticity, porosity, surface area, and functional-group density. The evidence repeatedly shows that higher temperature lowers yield and reduces hydrogen and oxygen, while increasing organic carbon, porosity, and recalcitrant carbon [N4-R1][N4-R4][N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-R4]. It also consistently links temperature to changes in surface groups and adsorption sites, indicating that functional-group density is another consistent variable [N3-F3][N5-F2]. The literature also consistently points to porosity and pore size distribution as temperature-sensitive properties [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Limitations and confounders remain in the literature. First, feedstock type strongly moderates temperature effects, so comparisons across studies may be invalid if feedstock differences are not controlled [N5-F2][N5-R2]. Second, temperature ranges are often defined broadly or operationally rather than as exact thresholds, which makes it difficult to compare results across studies [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R5]. Third, yield and volatiles interact with temperature effects, so lower yield at higher temperature can obscure whether the observed properties are due to temperature alone or to the loss of volatiles and functional groups [N4-R1][N2-R4]. Fourth, the evidence indicates that pyrolysis conditions such as heating rate, retention time, and pyrolytic atmosphere also influence biochar yield and surface functional groups, so temperature effects cannot be isolated from these variables [N2-R2][N5-F2]. Finally, the literature itself acknowledges uncertainty about the exact adjustment of production conditions and the precise relationship between temperature and biochar properties [N5-F2].

Overall, the consensus is that temperature has a clear directionality: higher temperature generally increases recalcitrant carbon, porosity, and surface area while decreasing yield, hydrogen, oxygen, and labile organics. However, the exact temperature effects depend heavily on feedstock, temperature range, and other process variables, which means that the literature remains somewhat mixed in comparison studies and that temperature should be interpreted alongside these confounders [N4-F1][N5-F2][N5-R2].

The chemical composition report emphasizes that higher pyrolysis temperature reduces concentrations of hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and labile organic carbon while increasing resistant carbon [N1-R2]. The DFT-based review reinforces this by stating that wood-based feedstock tends to yield biochar with more recalcitrant carbon and higher specific surface area, while straw-based feedstock preserves more oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen at lower temperatures [N5-F2]. It also notes that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, while higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and a higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. How temperature changes the chemical composition of biochar

The evidence points to a clear temperature-dependent evolution of biochar chemistry, with functional groups, oxygen content, aromaticity, and pyrolysis-stage decomposition all changing as temperature increases. Across the search results, biochar produced at higher pyrolysis temperatures is associated with lower concentrations of hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and labile organic carbon, while more resistant carbon structures dominate [N1-R2]. A separate search result similarly states that as pyrolysis temperature increases, weaker-bonded groups are progressively released, forming larger polyaromatic structures with lower hydrogen and oxygen [N1-R5]. This is consistent with the idea that higher temperature favors the condensation and aromatization of carbon, reducing the proportion of oxygen-containing functional groups and labile organics [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Functional groups are a central part of this compositional shift. The characterization literature notes that SEM, TEM, FTIR, BET surface area, and pore volume are commonly used to examine biochar structure, and FTIR spectra in one study revealed surface groups such as hydroxyls at ~3328 cm⁻¹, carboxyls at ~1703 cm⁻¹, and C=O or C=C contributions at ~1532 cm⁻¹ [N3-F3]. In the same context, the presence of hydroxyl, carboxyl, and other surface groups is tied to adsorption capacity because these groups interact with metals via hydrogen bonding and complexation [N3-F3]. The DFT-based review further emphasizes that functional groups such as hydroxyl (−OH), amino (−NH2), and carboxyl (−COOH) strongly influence biochar physicochemical properties and its interactions with soil substances [N5-F2]. This suggests that as temperature changes, these functional groups either persist, diminish, or restructure depending on the pyrolysis stage.

Aromaticity and oxygen content evolve in a predictable way across temperature ranges. Lower temperatures are associated with greater oxygen content, more functional groups, and higher hydrogen and oxygen concentrations, while higher temperatures are linked to lower oxygen content, greater aromatic carbon, and more recalcitrant structures [N1-R2][N1-R5]. The review explicitly states that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, whereas higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and a higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. Evidence for pyrolysis-stage effects on chemical composition comes from multiple sources. The evidence supports a clear pyrolysis-stage effect, with composition depending on whether the temperature is in the primary decomposition range, secondary degradation range, or carbonization range [N1-R4][N2-R3][N5-F2].

How temperature changes the chemical composition of biochar

The evidence points to a clear temperature-dependent evolution of biochar chemistry, with functional groups, oxygen content, aromaticity, and pyrolysis-stage decomposition all changing as temperature increases. Across the search results, biochar produced at higher pyrolysis temperatures is associated with lower concentrations of hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and labile organic carbon, while more resistant carbon structures dominate [N1-R2]. A separate search result similarly states that as pyrolysis temperature increases, weaker-bonded groups are progressively released, forming larger polyaromatic structures with lower hydrogen and oxygen [N1-R5]. This is consistent with the idea that higher temperature favors the condensation and aromatization of carbon, reducing the proportion of oxygen-containing functional groups and labile organics [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Functional groups are a central part of this compositional shift. The characterization literature notes that SEM, TEM, FTIR, BET surface area, and pore volume are commonly used to examine biochar structure, and FTIR spectra in one study revealed surface groups such as hydroxyls at ~3328 cm⁻¹, carboxyls at ~1703 cm⁻¹, and C=O or C=C contributions at ~1532 cm⁻¹ [N3-F3]. In the same context, the presence of hydroxyl, carboxyl, and other surface groups is tied to adsorption capacity because these groups interact with metals via hydrogen bonding and complexation [N3-F3]. The DFT-based review further emphasizes that functional groups such as hydroxyl (−OH), amino (−NH2), and carboxyl (−COOH) strongly influence biochar physicochemical properties and its interactions with soil substances [N5-F2]. This suggests that as temperature changes, these functional groups either persist, diminish, or restructure depending on the pyrolysis stage.

Aromaticity and oxygen content evolve in a predictable way across temperature ranges. Lower temperatures are associated with greater oxygen content, more functional groups, and higher hydrogen and oxygen concentrations, while higher temperatures are linked to lower oxygen content, greater aromatic carbon, and more recalcitrant structures [N1-R2][N1-R5]. The review explicitly states that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, whereas higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and a higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. This supports the conclusion that aromaticity tends to increase with temperature, while oxygen content decreases [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Evidence for pyrolysis-stage effects on chemical composition comes from multiple sources. One study notes that primary decomposition occurs in the temperature range of 200–350°C, while secondary degradation starts above 400°C [N1-R4]. Another study reports that increasing pyrolysis temperature progressively degrades organic matter and removes pore material, which is directly relevant to chemical composition changes [N2-R3]. The DFT review also frames pyrolysis temperature as the most significant manufacturing condition affecting biochar properties, with lower temperatures preserving functional groups and higher temperatures promoting recalcitrant carbon [N5-F2]. Together, these sources support a staged model of biochar formation: early-stage decomposition at lower temperatures releases labile organics and functional groups, while higher temperatures drive further aromatization and stabilization of carbon [N1-R4][N2-R3][N5-F2].

Temperature-dependent decomposition phases affect composition by altering the pathways through which biomass is converted. The evidence suggests that at lower temperatures, more volatile and labile components are retained, whereas at higher temperatures, volatiles are removed and carbonization proceeds, favoring aromatic and graphitic structures [N1-R4][N1-R5]. The comparison study also states that higher pyrolysis temperature produced products with higher organic carbon and a more developed structure, while lower temperature had lower yield and different properties [N4-R4]. This implies that decomposition phases are not simply thermal degradation but are also shaped by whether the system is in the primary or secondary pyrolysis regime [N1-R4][N4-R4].

Overall, the chemical composition of biochar changes systematically with pyrolysis temperature: lower temperatures preserve more oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and labile organics and retain functional groups; higher temperatures reduce these elements and increase aromaticity, recalcitrant carbon, and surface stability [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-F2]. The evidence supports a clear pyrolysis-stage effect, with composition depending on whether the temperature is in the primary decomposition range, secondary degradation range, or carbonization range [N1-R4][N2-R3][N5-F2].

Feedstock type moderates pyrolysis temperature effects in several ways. The evidence shows that different feedstocks can produce biochars with very different chemical and structural responses to temperature. The DFT-based review explicitly states that biochar derived from wood-based feedstock exhibits superior physical characteristics such as increased porosity and specific surface area, whereas biochar derived from straw-based feedstock contains excellent element content such as O, N, and H [N5-F2]. It also says that lower pyrolysis temperatures and straw-based feedstock can preserve surface functional groups better, while higher pyrolysis temperatures and wood-based feedstock result in more recalcitrant carbon and a higher specific surface area [N5-F2]. This indicates that feedstock composition and type strongly influence which temperature range produces the most desirable properties, such as high porosity, high surface area, or high oxygen content [N5-F2].

Operational differences between studies make comparisons valid only when temperature ranges, feedstocks, and characterization methods are comparable. The comparison study on agricultural waste biochar explicitly analyzes physical and chemical properties across pyrolysis temperatures and uses the same four materials (straw rice, sawdust, sugar cane plant residues, and tree leaves) under controlled conditions [N4-F1]. The review on feedstock and pyrolysis conditions also emphasizes that biochar yield is significantly influenced by operating temperature around 500°C, which corresponds to lignin decomposition or elimination of volatile matter [N5-R3]. This suggests that valid comparisons require attention to temperature windows, feedstock identity, and process conditions, because otherwise differences in yield, functional groups, and porosity can be misattributed to temperature alone [N4-F1][N5-R3].

Temperature ranges are typically defined in biochar literature as broad, overlapping intervals rather than exact thresholds. The evidence shows that pyrolysis temperature is often reported in ranges such as 200–350°C, 300–350°C, 400–500°C, 450–750°C, and 300–900°C, with some sources specifying subranges for primary and secondary decomposition [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. The review on recent advancements also states that fast pyrolysis is carried out at 450 to 600°C with a relatively higher heating rate, while slower processes may fall outside this range [N6-R4]. This indicates that temperature ranges are commonly used as approximate operational windows, not fixed cutoffs, and that studies often define them based on feedstock behavior, process design, or the point at which decomposition or carbonization becomes dominant [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4].

Yield and other process variables interact with temperature effects in several ways. First, yield is inversely related to temperature in the evidence: higher pyrolysis temperature results in lower yield, while lower temperature can preserve more volatiles and functional groups [N4-R1][N4-R4]. This implies that feedstock and process conditions are not just background variables; they are central to explaining why temperature effects differ between studies. For example, wood-based feedstock may respond to higher temperature with greater recalcitrant carbon and porosity, while straw-based feedstock may preserve more oxygen and functional groups at lower temperatures [N5-F2].

In short, feedstock type moderates temperature effects by altering the baseline chemistry, porosity, and functional groups available for pyrolysis [N5-F2]. Operational differences, including temperature range definitions, heating rate, retention time, and yield, make comparisons valid only when these variables are comparable across studies [N2-R2][N4-F1][N5-R3]. Temperature ranges are usually defined broadly as decomposition or carbonization windows rather than exact thresholds [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R5]. The evidence also consistently associates higher temperature with lower hydrogen and oxygen content, more aromaticity, and greater specific surface area or porosity [N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-R4][N5-F2]. A common theme is that temperature determines whether the material is in an early-decomposition regime or a carbonization-dominated regime, with the primary decomposition range often around 200–350°C and secondary degradation above 400°C [N1-R4].

Where studies disagree or show mixed results, the evidence suggests differences in feedstock and process conditions rather than fundamental inconsistency. For example, the comparison study on agricultural waste biochar explicitly analyzes physical and chemical properties across pyrolysis temperatures but does not report conflicting conclusions on temperature trends; instead, it emphasizes that physical and chemical properties vary with temperature and that feedstock choice affects the resulting properties [N4-F1]. The DFT-based review also notes that while qualitative correlations between pyrolysis temperature, feedstock properties, and biochar characteristics are established, there is still uncertainty regarding adjustment of production conditions and the exact relationships [N5-F2]. This implies that some studies may differ because they use different feedstocks, temperature windows, or pyrolysis atmospheres, rather than because temperature effects themselves are inconsistent [N5-F2].

The properties most consistently affected by temperature are yield, oxygen content, aromaticity, porosity, surface area, and functional-group density. The evidence repeatedly shows that higher temperature lowers yield and reduces hydrogen and oxygen, while increasing organic carbon, porosity, and recalcitrant carbon [N4-R1][N4-R4][N1-R2][N1-R5][N2-R4]. It also consistently links temperature to changes in surface groups and adsorption sites, indicating that functional-group density is another consistent variable [N3-F3][N5-F2]. The literature also consistently points to porosity and pore size distribution as temperature-sensitive properties [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Limitations and confounders remain in the literature. First, feedstock type strongly moderates temperature effects, so comparisons across studies may be invalid if feedstock differences are not controlled [N5-F2][N5-R2]. Second, temperature ranges are often defined broadly or operationally rather than as exact thresholds, which makes it difficult to compare results across studies [N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R5]. Third, yield and volatiles interact with temperature effects, so lower yield at higher temperature can obscure whether the observed properties are due to temperature alone or to the loss of volatiles and functional groups [N4-R1][N2-R4]. Fourth, the evidence indicates that pyrolysis conditions such as heating rate, retention time, and pyrolytic atmosphere also influence biochar yield and surface functional groups, so temperature effects cannot be isolated from these variables [N2-R2][N5-F2]. Finally, the literature itself acknowledges uncertainty about the exact adjustment of production conditions and the precise relationship between temperature and biochar properties [N5-F2].

Overall, the consensus is that temperature has a clear directionality: higher temperature generally increases recalcitrant carbon, porosity, and surface area while decreasing yield, hydrogen, oxygen, and labile organics. However, the exact temperature effects depend heavily on feedstock, temperature range, and other process variables, which means that the literature remains somewhat mixed in comparison studies and that temperature should be interpreted alongside these confounders [N4-F1][N5-F2][N5-R2].
